title: Turning off the antennae: nsrC suppresses phycobilisome biosynthesis during nitrogen starvation
content: Nitrogen is an essential element for life and is frequently limiting in the environment. Although many cyanobacteria are diazotrophic and can convert atmospheric N2 into usable forms, non-diazotrophic cyanobacteria are unable to utilize atmospheric N2 and instead rely on dissolved nitrogen sources, such as ammonium, nitrate, and amino acids. In these species, nitrogen limitation reduces growth and photosynthetic activity and triggers extensive metabolic reprogramming (Inabe et al. 2021). One key mechanism for adapting to low nitrogen levels is the targeted degradation of proteins, which releases amino acids that can be recycled for use in critical processes associated with nitrogen limitation responses. Phycobilisomes, the major pigment-protein antenna complexes in cyanobacteria and red algae, are prominent targets of this response. Their structural components, including phycocyanin, allophycocyanin, and linker proteins, are degraded during nitrogen starvation, releasing substantial amounts of amino acids, which reduces their light-harvesting capacity and is manifest as chlorosis or a loss of pigmentation (Spät et al. 2018).
